pr_body:
#12217 an #12276 taught us that errno codes aren't necessarily organised as a small sequential set of numbers.  In fact, POSIX stipulates that the macros should be used for the codes and that no other assumptions can be made.

We therefore need to rethink how we pack errno codes into our own `ERR_LIB_SYS` codes.  This may prove more dodgy than we can handle somewhere in the future, but for the moment, the changes made here are hopefully enough to handle what we currently know.

This change also deals with an overlap of `ERR_R_` codes (which has already appeared as strange error messages)

Finally, we change `test/errtest.c` to use `EPERM` instead of `1`.

Fixes #12217 
Fixes #12276 

-----

This is an alternative to #12289, using similar ideas for the codes.

It's also for all other possibilities.  We had problems previously on Windows, see how I removed the Windows specific hackery from `02-test_errstr.t`.

Also, most of the work is not hurd specific, but is meant to generalise in a more future proof manner.  Plus it deals with certain reason code overlaps that haven't been dealt with for eons (I'm surprised no one else noticed)

Yeah, I was thinking of that, mostly because it exists in two places.  We still need a stable source if E macro names, which could be a perl script that takes them from the Errno module.

> The base problem is that OpenSSL doesn't allow enough bits for errno on some platforms. This doesn't seem to address the fact that, for example, errno is allowed to be an int. I would expect an explicit errno field added

The base problem is that we have all kinds of info packed into an `int`.  We *could* have a small struct that we pass around by value (this is supported in C) instead, and thereby allow the reason code to take on the full size of an `int`.

Yes, you could turn error into a struct if you didn't care about "most applications will just need to recompile."

My proposal solves the root problem simply.  Want a PR?

Uhmmmmm, how exactly did you mean to do that?  After all, functions like `ERR_peek_error`, `ERR_error_string`, the `ERR_GET_` functions/macros all return or expect a complete packed error code (i.e that includes the library code and the reason code, and formerly the function code).
I read the code, and perhaps I'm just missing something, but how does this PR not return a truncated error code?

The added `err_pack()` repacks hurd error codes by taking away the middle bits. In concrete terms, the code xxyyzztt is re-packed to xxzztt, because it turns out that yy is 00, or ff for negative errors, and is therefore not significant. 

For all other platforms, it is indeed truncated to the lowest 24 bits of errno. As far as I have seen so far, that shouldn't be a problem, but if it is, adding code to re-pack another platform's code in `err_pack` should be fairly simple, and if it turns out not to be true, we'll take the problem then.

I still feel that this is a hack for a non-common platform, but oh well.

For the OpenSSL-internal representation for the POSIX error codes
better use the index of the values held in the `known_codes` array.
This way the encoding is optimal (in the sense of minimal size) 
and no assumption is needed about the external encoding of the values.

Note that according to <https://pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/9699919799/basedefs/errno.h.html> 
the only assumption we can make about the external encoding  is that they are distinct positive values.

In other words, 
simply re-enumerate the defined POSIX error names/macros and use the resulting values as their internal encoding. 
In this way we are entirely independent of the encoding defined in `errno.h` and the max value is as small as
```
#define NUM_SYS_STR_REASONS OSSL_NELEM(known_codes) - 1
```

Re `UNKNOWN_ERRNO`...  so far, we have had the reason text `reason(nnn)` with the actual reason number for any error where we don't have a text.  So for an errno 132 that we hadn't got a text for, we would display `reason(132)`, which gave people a chance to find out what's going on even if we couldn't tell.  Maybe people don't care, I dunno, but suddenly serving them a generic "we have no clue" error text feels...  like a bit of a downgrade.

I have no idea if I'm over inflating the issue...

> > Correct that for this use case likely an inefficient search (or some fancy optimization) is needed,
> > but this is done rarely (only when preparing error output).

> Er, no, it would happen any time ERR_set_error() is called (which happens at the SYSerr() / ERR_raise_data() calls), because it needs to pack that as a reason code into the error record.

This is what I meant by "preparing error output".
That is, only when an error situation has been detected, which may be at many *places* in the code,
but not often in terms of run-time *execution*, such that an inefficient search called at this point should not be a problem.

> apps/lib/apps.c:        ERR_raise_data(ERR_LIB_SYS, errno,
> crypto/bio/b_addr.c:                ERR_raise_data(ERR_LIB_SYS, get_last_socket_error(),
> crypto/bio/b_addr.c:            ERR_raise_data(ERR_LIB_SYS, get_last_socket_error(),
> ...

Right, but even if there are many such occurrences this is not an efficiency problem.

The mapping of the POSIX error code to the internal one would be done in (an updated version of) `err_pack()`,
which is stable and independent of the OS, without the need for brittle hacks like 
```
#ifdef __gnu_hurd__
        /*
         * GNU hurd appears to use an error code structure where the top 4
         * bits and the bottom 16 bits are significant, the middle bits are
         * not.  With that in mind, we can compress the Hurd codes to fit
         * 24 bits.
         */
        reason = ((reason >> 8UL) & 0x00FF0000L) | (reason & 0x0000FFFFL);
#endif
```

1. If the `errno` value is found in the enumeration table we record internally a new pseudo-lib code (such as `ERR_LIB_ERRNO`) and the found enumeration index (which is < `NUM_SYS_STR_REASONS`) and have a mnemonic text to display.

2. In the (not very likely) case that the `errno` value is not found in the enumeration table,
we can display for instance `UNKNOWN_ERRNO=132` in analogy to your above example.
To this end we can record internally, similarly as before,
`ERR_LIB_SYS` and `errno & 0xffffff` (since unfortunately we only have 24 bits at our disposal),
 hoping that this gives somewhat useful info to any interested user.

> But for your consideration, we have always assumed something "well-known"... before this PR, the assumption has been that the errno range is 1..127 (which is a false assumption if you listen to POSIX).

A known *range* is very different from a known list of codepoints. Of course 127 is rather tight. With glibc on Fedora 31, the current highest errno is 133.  The real problem is packing errno values into less than 32 bits, the real solution has to be to stop doing that, not make up some ad-hoc compression scheme.

> As @richsalz points out, we could generate it on a per-system basis. But for your consideration, we have always assumed something "well-known"... before this PR, the assumption has been that the errno range is 1..127 (which is a false assumption if you listen to POSIX).

Yes - as already mentioned above, the problem (to be) addressed in this PR is that according to <https://pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/9699919799/basedefs/errno.h.html> the *only* assumptions that we can safely make on the `errno` values are that 
they are defined as macros which shall expand to **integer constant expressions with type `int`, distinct positive values**.
In earlier times, the guarantees were even weaker (namely, that they are non-zero values).

So am I to get this right, that we should only do the indirect errno solution on platforms where we *know* that they don't fit in 20 bits?  Is a pre-defined table of mappings acceptable in that case?  What should we do with errno's that aren't in that table?

> So am I to get this right, that we should only do the indirect errno solution on platforms where we _know_ that they don't fit in 20 bits? Is a pre-defined table of mappings acceptable in that case? What should we do with errno's that aren't in that table?

It would not feel right to me, also from the usage perspective, to make a case distinction between systems where (it looks like that) the `errno` values fit in 20 bits and where not. 

> Might it make sense to restrict the solution to the problem platforms? Otherwise the errno value may need to be removed from the OpenSSL error object, and stored separately.

Meanwhile I think the most straightforward solution would be (regardless of the system) to record in our 32-bit error code only the *fact* that a system error occurred and 
let our default error queue printing code, as well anyone else interested in the details, simply consult `errno` by calling an accessor function like `get_last_socket_error()`.

> let our default error queue printing code, as well anyone else interested in the details, simply consult `errno` by calling an accessor function like `get_last_socket_error()`.

What makes you think the errno has been  preserved all the way 'til `ERR_print_errors` or similar is called?  Or when something as simple as `ERR_GET_REASON()` is called?

> What makes you think the errno has been preserved all the way 'til `ERR_print_errors` or similar is called? Or when something as simple as `ERR_GET_REASON()` is called?

Ah, right, we'll need to copy and store it along with the respective error queue entry.

> Ah, right, we'll need to copy and store it along with the respective error queue entry.

This is the solution that @richsalz proposed, but there are issues with that proposal, i.e. all the functions that *pop the error off the queue* (such as `ERR_get_error_all`, which is used in `ERR_print_errors_cb`)...  you get the recorded error code, and the queued entry is essentially gone (it may still be there, but it may also be overwritten by another recorded error), so if you have an indirect reason that expects the real reason code to be in the queued entry, we have a problem.

Thus I don't see this issue as a valid argument against any way of storing (most of) the `errno` value along with the queue entry.

Er, I have no idea how you see this as a path going forward.  With such a solution, we're fixing one issue by *knowingly* introducing another much more complex issue.

> above of that, also the solution to somehow squeeze the `errno` value in the error code would have the same issue.

I disagree.  There's a huge difference between a squeeze that gives *some* value and loosing that value altogether.

The situation could, of course, be resolved by changing the ERR sub-system to have a larger type for the packed error code.  Say, uint64_t.  Unfortunately, we've promised to stay source compatible, so we're stuck with 32-bit values.

@levitte 
Looks like there is some misunderstanding among us here. I'll try to be a little more detailed/explicit:

The issue I just mentioned above as a side note, namely that we only offer queue-like access to the error queue entries, not allowing random access, is not something that I propose to change (nor to discuss further) here.

The issue that (the copy of) the `errno` value, when stored along with a queue entry indicating a system error, can become inaccessible by chopping off queue entries, is independent of how in detail the value is stored.
Or which essential difference do you see in this respect comparing the approaches discussed so far, which can be summarized as follows?

1 Store the whole errno value in a separate queue entry component as suggested by @richsalz, which I meanwhile favor.

2a Store a (depending on the system, potentially somewhat squeezed) version of the errno value in the lower 20 bits of the err code, as currently done by you in this PR.

2b Store in the lower 20 bits of the err code an index of the errno value as far as it is known to us, else its lower 20 bits (as I had suggested yesterday and adapted by you from 24 to 20 bits).

I think the core problem cannot be solved the "right way" without breaking source compatibility, which means it would have to wait for a future release.  Until then, it seems that only GNU HURD is affected (the rest are theoretical), which doesn't seem to be an important platform right now.
There are parts of this PR that isn't about Hurd...  I'll break them apart so they can be reviewed separately.

or is this just a consequence for the textual representation of the
error code?

Sebastian

We pre-load the error strings to fit into our error string structure.  Previous to this PR, we simply used the range 1..127, which doesn't fit what you'd expect on Hurd, since the POSIX numbers (which are the most commonly used) are in the range 0x40000001..0x40000079 (according to https://github.com/lattera/glibc/blob/master/sysdeps/mach/hurd/bits/errno.h), so for Hurd, we're entirely missing the target.
I've moved the non-Hurd bits to #12343

So I had another wild...  but workable thought last evening.  This comes from the fact that errno value shall fit in a `int` *and be positive*, so for a 32-bit `int`, they have the range 0x1..0x7fffffff.

So what if we seriously played with bits (something we should be quite good at, all things considered :wink:), and encoded our error records as follows?

System errors:

```
<---------------------------- 32 bits -------------------------->
+-+-------------------------------------------------------------+
|1|                  system error number (31 b)                 |
+-+-------------------------------------------------------------+
```

OpenSSL errors:

```
<---------------------------- 32 bits -------------------------->
+-+---------------+---------------------------------------------+
|0| library (8 b) |                  reason (23 b)              |
+-+---------------+---------------------------------------------+
```

No system error number crunching needed whatsoever.  Only one flipped bit, which is easily special cased in our error code, and even in our ERR_GET macros.

I also wonder, why do we pre-load the system errors?  Yeah ok, if we want to make it easily fit in OpenSSL error messages without special casing anything...  but if we go along with my wilder idea, isn't that a moot point?  That saves us from the whole sys string reason array mess, just call openssl_strerror_r() when we actually need the string.

I'd like to bring in just two minor further tweaks:
1. Use the 0 bit for the `errno` value, such that our error code then reads identical to it:

  +-+-------------------------------------------------------------+
  |0|                  system error number (31 b)                 |
  +-+-------------------------------------------------------------+
  ```

  <---------------------------- 32 bits -------------------------->
  +-+---------------+---------------------------------------------+
  |1| library (7 b) |                  reason (24 b)              |
  +-+---------------+---------------------------------------------+
  ```

Sorry for being the wise guy, but the original proverb is slightly different:

> **Umgekehrt** wird ein Schuh draus.

The word "umgekehrt" has a dual meaning as "Reversed, ..." (in the literal sense) and "Conversely, ..." (in the figurative sense):

The literal meaning is:

> You need to "reverse" the leather to (sew it from both sides and) produce a high quality shoe.


The figurative meaning is

> You need to "think around the corner"  (change your viewpoint, think the other way around) to obtain a good result.

See for example this [explanation in german], or its [english google translation].

[explanation in german]: https://www.swr.de/wissen/1000-antworten/kultur/1000-antworten-2818.html
